title: Latency-brokered Toolcall Patterns & Slim SDK Surface (WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an experimental PRD-level sketch for a lightweight SDK surface and server-side broker that negotiates latency vs. fidelity for streaming tool-calls and structured output. Focus is on making it easy for product engineers to adopt streaming tool workflows with minimal integration friction while giving the platform levers to preserve latency SLOs and reduce cost.

Context / problem space:
- Customers want SDK patterns that make tool invocation feel native (low-latency, resumable, and debuggable) while avoiding heavy client-side state machines.
- Large hosted streaming sessions sometimes trigger expensive synchronous tool calls that blow past latency budgets. We need explicit patterns and a small runtime "broker" that brokers tool calls across latency tiers and returns graceful partial structured responses.
- Existing SDKs require too much boilerplate for fallback, speculative prefetch, and structured output validation.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Provide a 1-API, low-boilerplate SDK surface for streaming + tool-calls that supports: incremental partial responses, tool-call hedging, speculative-prefetch hints, and structured output frames.
- Server-side broker can categorize tool calls into latency tiers (fast, best-effort, background), enforce per-request latency budget, and return partial structured frames when tools are slow/fail.
- Reduce median end-to-end toolcall latency for interactive clients by 20% in high contention scenarios via hedging/prefetch policies.
- SDK ergonomics: <10 lines to enable a streaming toolflow; clear primitives for attach/detach, resume, and structured-output parsing.

Non-goals:
- Full replacement for heavy orchestration (e.g., complex long-running workflows, multi-tool transactional sagas).
- Implementing full client-side graph orchestration (we provide primitives, not a complete DAG engine).

Key user stories:
- As a product engineer embedding a chat UI, I want the model to call a calendar API and show the user a "best guess" within 150ms, with the accurate response following as a discrete structured patch when available.
- As an SDK user, I want a single call to the hosted API that streams model tokens, tool-call events, and structured output frames without needing a separate websocket for tools.
- As an operator, I want the ability to define per-customer latency tiers and cost tradeoffs so that dedicated customers can opt into expensive synchronous calls while free-tier requests get hedged/evicted earlier.

Constraints & assumptions:
- Clients prefer websockets (or HTTP/2 streaming) but SDK should abstract transport.
- Server-side broker can access cached KV prefixes and reuse recent tool results for speculative hints.
- Tool endpoints are heterogeneous (internal microservices, external SaaS). A small timeout-based classification will be necessary.

High-level approach (components):
- Slim SDK: single client API for streaming sessions. Exposes: session.createStream(), on('token'), on('tool_event'), on('structured_frame'), resume(session_id).
- Latency Broker (hosted): intercepts tool-call requests emitted by the serving runtime, classifies calls into latency tiers, applies policies (hedge, prefetch, background), and emits structured frames back into the same streaming session.
- Structured Frame Schema: minimal typed envelope for partial results: {frame_id, frame_type, status, payload_schema_version, payload}. (We will include example small JSON-LD-like envelope in examples below.)

Policy primitives (server side):
- budget_ms: total allowable tool latency for request (configurable per plan).
- hedge_window_ms: speculative hedging start time for redundant calls (when multiple compatible backends exist).
- fallback_mode: enum {partial_frame, null_hint, deferred_attachment}.
- prefetch_hint: boolean (broker may pre-run fast cached lookups).

SDK ergonomic patterns (examples):
- Basic streaming + tools (Node-ish pseudocode):
  const s = client.createStream({model: 'rwd-chat-1', budget_ms: 250});
  s.on('token', t => renderToken(t));
  s.on('tool_event', e => {
    if (e.type === 'tool_call') showSpinnerForTool(e.tool_id);
    if (e.type === 'tool_result') showToolResult(e.tool_id, e.payload);
  });
  s.on('structured_frame', f => applyPatchFrames(f));
  await s.start(prompt);

- Resume semantics: sessions produce checkpoint frames (compact cursor + KV hash). The SDK should expose a resume(session_id, cursor) that attaches to the same live stream or returns aggregated frames for replay.

Server-to-client event types (stream frames):
- token: incremental model text token
- tool_call: model requested a tool, includes tool_id, call_id, input_schema, prefer_latency_tier
- tool_result: canonical result (full fidelity)
- partial_tool_result: partial/approximate result when tool exceeds tier (synthesized or cached)
- structured_frame: typed patch describing application-visible state (e.g., calendar_event_added)
- heartbeat & diagnostics: escape hatch for SDKs to surface latency debug info

Example sequence (user-facing):
1) Client opens stream; model emits tokens: "I can add that to your calendar — " then tool_call{calendar_write, prefer_latency:fast}
2) Broker evaluates: direct calendar API likely 600ms (slow). Since budget_ms=250, broker emits partial_tool_result with "tentative-event: 2026-01-12 10:00" and structured_frame status=partial. SDK shows "Added tentatively" in UI.
3) Tool finishes; broker emits tool_result and updated structured_frame with status=final and canonical id. UI replaces tentative with canonical.

Error & fallback behaviors (client-facing):
- If tool_error: broker emits structured_frame with status=error and optional error metadata (retryable flag). SDK surface shows inline retry CTA.
- If budget exceeded and no partial available: fallback_mode dictates (null_hint = skip tool and continue; partial_frame = synthesize best-effort placeholder).

Observability & telemetry hooks:
- Token-level latency histogram per session, tool-call timings (queued, in-flight, hedge latencies), cache hit/miss rates for prefetch, and partial->final delta timings.
- SDK should emit minimal telemetry (client visible) to identify stuck sessions: last_event_ts, last_toolcall_id.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0: internal PoC with SDK prototype + broker in staging. Validate sequence semantics and structured_frame envelope.
- Phase 1: limited beta with selected customers (internal integrations team + 3 customers). Collect SLO impact metrics.
- Phase 2: GA with opt-in toggles per-project: "allow speculative partials", "aggressive hedging", "strict sync".

Open questions / trade-offs to discuss:
- How much server-side synthesis is acceptable as a "partial" result without violating data contracts? (privacy & correctness concerns)
- Structured frame shape: do we enforce a strict JSON schema per tool or allow freeform payload with type tags? (tradeoff: client parsing safety vs. flexibility)
- Billing semantics: partial frames may misrepresent resource consumption if we report optimistic success before final tool runs. Need billing guardrails.

Next actions (owner: Ava):
- Wire up a tiny Node SDK prototype that exposes the event callbacks (target: 3-day spike).
- Define minimal structured_frame envelope and basic unit tests for resume semantics (target: 1 week).
- Draft a short telemetry contract with SRE: event names and tags for toolcall latency (target: 1 week).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is lightweight sketch intended to spark engineering debate — it intentionally keeps the SDK small and pushes complexity to the broker so clients remain thin. Expect follow-ups to refine schemas and error cases.

References / related tickets:
- Linear RED-4123: "tool-call hedging and budget enforcement"
- GH PR: hosted-sdk/#184 (streaming hooks experiment)

Quick mental model (for design reviews):
- Think of the broker as a low-latency concierge: it buffers, classifies, and decides whether to wait, hedge, or emit a best-effort frame. The SDK is a low-latency renderer that receives tokens and frames and lets the product app choose how to display tentative vs. final data.

-- end of sketch --
